text: RBAC tells you how to grant access to a role. Least privilege tells you how much that role's permission list should actually contain, every account gets the minimum access required to do its job, nothing added for convenience, nothing kept just in case.

The test is simple to state: for every permission on a role, can you name the specific task that requires it? If the answer is no, but it might be useful someday, that permission shouldn't be there. Just-in-case access feels harmless in the moment, but when that account gets phished or its credentials leak, every permission it holds becomes available to whoever controls it.

Permission creep is least privilege eroding gradually instead of being violated all at once. Someone moves between three teams over four years, and each move adds the new team's access, but nobody removes the old team's, because that's a separate, easy-to-skip step. After four years, they hold the union of everything they've ever needed, far more than their current job requires. That's exactly the Mover failure mode from Joiner-Mover-Leaver, and access reviews exist largely to catch it.

Least privilege applies to time, not just scope. Just-in-time elevation grants a powerful permission only for the window it's needed, then automatically revokes it, a DBA requests sysadmin rights for a specific maintenance window instead of holding them permanently. Security teams call the scope of damage a compromised credential can cause its blast radius, and least privilege is the primary lever for shrinking it.

A tightly scoped account can only touch what its job needed if it's compromised. A broadly permissioned one can touch everything it ever touched. Next up: segregation of duties, splitting powerful actions across more than one person.
